description:
We’re Apollogistics, a team that apologises for nothing except the name. 
Just kidding, we are Apollogistics and we are here to help you with your lunar logistics. We built a “Google Moon” for mission planners: pick your rover’s limits, and it searches NASA terrain for the days and spots with sunlight, a line to Earth and power to spare. Then you can stand there, in your browser or a VR headset. Still happy to debate whether you mean degrees or radians.
summary:
March 6th, 2025. A robot the size of a dishwasher finishes a million kilometre trip to the Moon’s south pole. It’s carrying a drill, to look for water: the water people will one day drink there.
It misses its target by 250 metres, and falls into a crater.
Lying on its side, it sends one last picture. Earth, hanging in the black sky. It could see home. It could not see the Sun. Thirteen hours later, it went silent.
In 2027 another rover goes to the same place. VIPER was built, cancelled, and saved. It gets one landing. Fifty hours of darkness, and it never wakes up.

No app could have caught Athena. But every team chooses a place and a day. And at the south pole, that choice decides whether your rover wakes up.
Lunar Landing Site Navigator flips the planning question. You tell it what your rover can survive. It searches NASA’s LOLA terrain across seven south-pole regions, follows the Sun and Earth hour by hour for 30 days, and answers with a landing date and place: days of unbroken sunlight, time with Earth in view, estimated solar power, and why the other days fail. Then you can stand at the site in 3D or VR.

Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.004°. When a launch slips, a team can re-check 15,120 possible landings on one screen, and students can see for themselves why the south pole is so hard.
details:
The problem is that water ice at the Moon’s south pole hides in craters the Sun never reaches, but a rover needs sunlight to live and Earth in view to be driven. The Sun there sits a degree or two above the horizon, so one ridge can mean days of darkness. In March 2025 the Athena lander ended up 250 m off target in a crater and lost about 95% of its planned mission. NASA’s VIPER rover, to be delivered by Blue Origin in late 2027, cannot endure more than 50 hours of continuous darkness. And launches slip: every slip moves the Sun, the shadows and the view of Earth.

What it does it do? You describe the mission: how long the rover survives darkness, how accurately the lander lands, how steep it can drive. The app searches seven south-pole regions (NASA’s Artemis III candidates) and returns landing sites and a landing time, with days of unbroken sunlight, the share of the stay with Earth in view, an estimate of solar power and battery need, and a 30-day strip showing why each failing day fails. It then plans a rover drive, and lets you stand at the site in a 3D street view or a VR headset, with the Sun and Earth where they would really be.

This is how it works: NASA’s LOLA terrain is turned into a skyline for each spot: the highest ground in 720 compass directions, out to 300 km, with the Moon’s curvature. Sun and Earth positions are computed for every hour and compared with that skyline. Every landing hour for 30 days is tested against the rover’s rules, up to 15,120 landings per mission. Power is sunlight strength × panel area × efficiency × the angle to the Sun × the share of the Sun’s disc above the ridge.

Benefits and impacts: A mission team can re-check a slipped launch on one screen instead of stitching expert tools together by hand. It also shows design consequences early: at one site, the same panel makes about 375 W upright and under 10 W lying flat. Students and museum visitors can walk the south pole on real NASA terrain.

Most tools online show the sky for a date you already chose. Ours works backwards, from the rover’s limits to the dates and places that keep it alive, and then puts you there.

What we considered: we state the limits: terrain is 80 m per pixel (5 m at four sites), so rocks are invisible, results are hourly; Earth in view means a direct link is possible, not guaranteed; power is an estimate. Positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to 0.004°, and 289 automated tests cover the code.

Tools used and included: JavaScript, HTML and CSS; three.js and WebXR for 3D and VR; Astronomy Engine for Sun and Earth positions; Vite and Node.js; Vitest. AI coding assistants helped write and review code, tests and documentation; the team directed the design and checked the results.
dataRefs: LOLA 5 m south-pole maps (NASA Goddard PGDA)
